I didn't write any dependency rules. Enforcement can't run until the notifications subsystem has a decided place in the architecture, and you've said it doesn't have one yet.

**What I found:** Writing the rules has to wait (the record calls this Defer). Dependency rules say which layers and subsystems notifications may import and which may import it. Without a decided placement there is nothing to encode. The pipeline blocks enforcement until the placement stage (L) has accepted a placement.

**Why it matters:** Rules written now would encode a guess. If the placement comes out differently, they would either flag correct imports as violations or let wrong ones through. Both make the rules unreliable from the first commit. Also, the rule files for a new subsystem have to ship in the same PR as its code, so nothing is lost by waiting.

**Do this first:**
1. Run `/alchemy L place a new notifications subsystem`. It decides the domain, layer and allowed directions, and runs a complexity measurement before accepting.

Then run `/alchemy E` on that accepted placement to write the rule file.

**What I did not check:** I didn't read the enforcement skill (`architecture-as-code`) or look for existing rule files (`eslint.architecture.mjs` / `architecture.toml`), because enforcement stops before either is needed. I also didn't search for an earlier placement decision, since you stated placement isn't decided. If one exists, point E at it and E can go ahead.

```
Dispatch:   DIRECT
Core route: E (blocked at prerequisite; not run)
Companions: None
Execution:  single-agent — single focused gate
Verdict:    Defer
Reason:     E requires an accepted L placement; notifications has none. Rules without a placement encode a guess.
Next:       /alchemy L place a new notifications subsystem, then /alchemy E on the accepted placement
```
